chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.keys: Make focused, distraction-free work the center of your career, and protect time for it this week. Newport calls this deep work: hard concentration with no distractions that pushes your thinking to its limit, creates new value and is hard for anyone else to copy. Its opposite is shallow work: logistical, low-effort tasks often done while distracted, which add little value and are easy to replace. His deep work hypothesis is that this ability is getting rarer at the same time it is getting more valuable, so the few who build it will thrive. The book first makes the case for deep work, then gives four rules for training it. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Carl Jung built a stone tower retreat at Bollingen to think without interruption, and Newport lines him up with other thinkers who walled off time for hard work. Jason Benn, a finance worker who saw his job could be done by spreadsheet scripts, shut himself away to learn programming deeply and landed a developer job.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Valuable
chapters.keys: Build the two abilities that pay in this economy, and build them by working deeply. Newport borrows the idea of the Great Restructuring, where smart machines split the economy and three groups win: high-skilled workers who can work with intelligent machines, superstars who are the best at what they do, and owners with capital. To join the first two groups you need two core abilities: learning hard things fast, and producing at an elite level in quality and speed. Learning hard things takes deliberate practice, meaning tight focus on one skill plus feedback, and he says focused attention is what builds the myelin that makes skills stick. Producing at an elite level follows a rule he states: high-quality work equals time spent times intensity of focus. Attention residue, part of your mind staying stuck on the last task after you switch, drags down your work, so long single-task stretches beat hopping between things. Reversal: Newport admits some people, such as top executives like Jack Dorsey, succeed while constantly interrupted, but he treats this as a narrow exception. Story the author tells: Adam Grant became the youngest full professor at Wharton by batching his teaching into one semester and his research into long stretches when he cut himself off from contact.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Rare
chapters.keys: Do not adopt the habits your workplace pushes, like open offices, constant instant messaging and being always online, just because everyone does. Newport names the metric black hole: the cost of distraction is hard to measure, so companies ignore it. He names the principle of least resistance: without clear feedback on what a behavior costs, people do what is easiest in the moment, like staying always connected. He names busyness as a proxy for productivity: when no one can show clear output, people look busy instead. He also names the cult of the internet, the habit of treating anything online as good by default. Because these forces keep most people shallow, deep work is rare, and that rarity is the opportunity. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Tom Cochran, chief technology officer at Atlantic Media, tallied his own email and estimated that email cost his company over a million dollars a year in employee time.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Meaningful
chapters.keys: Treat your knowledge work as a craft and go deep, because depth makes work meaningful, not just productive. Newport gives three arguments. Neurological: what you pay attention to shapes how your life feels, so focusing on deep work builds a better inner world. Psychological: people are happiest in flow, fully stretched by a hard task, and this happens more often at work than in leisure, and deep work produces flow. Philosophical: doing a craft well can bring meaning without needing some outside sacred order. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Ric Furrer, a blacksmith, forges a sword with total concentration, the model Newport holds up for knowledge workers. Winifred Gallagher, after a cancer diagnosis, chose to focus her attention on what was good in her life and found her life felt better.

chapters.title: Work Deeply
chapters.keys: Do not rely on willpower to go deep; build routines and rituals that do it for you, because willpower is limited and runs out as you use it. Choose a depth philosophy: monastic (cut out almost all shallow work), bimodal (block off long deep stretches, stay open the rest), rhythmic (deep work at the same time every day, a habit chain) or journalistic (drop into deep work whenever a gap opens). Ritualize: set where you work, how long, what rules apply, and what supports you. Make grand gestures, big costly moves that signal the work matters. Do not work alone: mix ideas in shared spaces, the hub-and-spoke model. Execute like a business: focus on the wildly important, act on lead measures, keep a visible scoreboard, review regularly. Be lazy: stop at the end of the day with a shutdown ritual, checking every open task, making a plan for it and saying a set phrase, because a plan quiets unfinished tasks and downtime recharges the attention deep work uses. Reversal: Newport says the monastic philosophy fits only people whose value comes from one clear output, and most people should pick another. Story the author tells: J.K. Rowling checked into a luxury Edinburgh hotel suite to finish the last Harry Potter book, a grand gesture; Donald Knuth gave up email so he could work monastically.

chapters.title: Embrace Boredom
chapters.keys: Train your focus like a muscle, and stop grabbing your phone at every bored moment. Newport reports research by Clifford Nass that heavy multitaskers lose the ability to filter out what does not matter; a brain wired for distraction keeps craving it. Don't take breaks from distraction, take breaks from focus: schedule in advance the blocks when you may go online, and stay offline outside them, even at home. Work like Teddy Roosevelt: set a hard, short deadline for a task and attack it at full intensity. Meditate productively: take one hard work problem with you on a walk or drive and keep pulling your mind back to it. Memorize a deck of cards: memory training builds the power to concentrate. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Teddy Roosevelt at Harvard packed his studying into short intense bursts and kept the rest of his day for other interests; Daniel Kilov struggled to focus as a student and trained his memory.

chapters.title: Quit Social Media
chapters.keys: Choose your online tools on purpose and cut the ones that do not serve your main goals. Newport rejects the any-benefit approach, using a tool if you can find any benefit at all while ignoring what it costs. He offers the craftsman approach: name the few things that drive your success and happiness, and keep a tool only if its benefits clearly outweigh its harms on those things. Apply the law of the vital few: a small number of activities produce most of the results, so judge tools by whether they support those. Quit social media for thirty days without telling anyone, then ask whether those days would have been notably better with it and whether anyone noticed you were gone. Don't use the internet to entertain yourself: plan your free time with real activities instead of drifting online. Reversal: if the thirty-day test shows a service really mattered, Newport says go back to it. Story the author tells: Baratunde Thurston, a heavy social media user, took about twenty-five days off all of it and found the break worthwhile.

chapters.title: Drain the Shallows
chapters.keys: Treat shallow work with suspicion, cap it hard, and spend the freed time on deep work. Schedule every minute of your day: plan your workday in blocks on paper and rewrite the plan when it breaks. Quantify the depth of every activity: ask how many months it would take to train a smart new graduate to do the task; short answers mean shallow. Ask your boss for a shallow work budget, an agreed share of your time for shallow tasks. Finish your work by 5:30: fixed-schedule productivity, setting a firm end time and working backward, forces you to cut shallow work. Become hard to reach: make people who email you do more work, write your own emails to close the loop in one go, and do not reply to everything. Reversal: Newport says you cannot remove shallow work entirely; some of it has to be done. Story the author tells: 37signals tried a four-day work week in summer and still got the work done; Newport says the lesson is that much of the time was shallow and should have gone to deep work. He also describes his own practice of rarely working past 5:30 while keeping up his research output.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.keys: Commit to a deep life: build your work around focus, and you get both results and meaning. Newport says this takes hard effort and real changes to your habits. He applied the rules himself while writing the book and reports a productive year from them. Reversal: Newport says a deep life is not for everybody, because of the effort and changes it demands. Story the author tells: Bill Gates, working with Paul Allen, spent about eight weeks of intense focus writing a version of BASIC for the Altair, an early personal computer, and that work helped launch Microsoft.
